01.title: Digital Marketing Jobs in Mauritius: The Skills Employers Want in 2026
segs:
Scroll through digital marketing jobs in Mauritius today and you'll notice something odd.

The job titles look simple. "Digital Marketing Executive." "Community Manager." "SEO Specialist." But open the listings and the requirements read like three jobs rolled into one.

Google Ads and Meta Ads. Google Analytics. SEO tools. Content, design, reporting. English and French. And, more and more, an understanding of AI.

If you're a graduate, a job seeker or thinking about a career change, that can feel overwhelming. It shouldn't. Once you see the pattern behind these marketing jobs in Mauritius, you can plan exactly what to learn and in what order.

In this article, I'll walk you through the roles that exist locally, the skills and tools employers keep asking for, how to build a portfolio before your first job, and how AI is changing all of it.

Key takeaways

  • Local employers hire for social media, paid ads, SEO, content, analytics, e-commerce and CRM, often combined in one role.
  • The tools that come up again and again: Google Analytics, Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, Search Console, SEMrush or Ahrefs, WordPress and Canva.
  • English and French are frequently listed as essential, and Mauritian Creole can be a plus.
  • Employers ask for portfolios and campaign examples, so you need proof of work, not just a certificate.
  • AI is already in the job ads: SEO roles now mention GEO, AEO and AI-powered search.

What digital marketing jobs in Mauritius actually look like

I spent time reading current listings on myjob.mu, one of the main job boards here. A few patterns jumped out straight away.

First, most roles are hybrids. Mauritian companies are rarely big enough to hire a separate person for every channel, so one marketer often covers social, ads, SEO and reporting.

Second, the same handful of roles keeps appearing. Here's what each one involves.

1. Social media and community manager

This is the most common entry point. A recent listing from a local retailer describes the job as running social channels, replying to messages and feedback, creating content and tracking engagement. Previous experience is "an advantage", not a requirement.

Community management is also growing beyond Facebook and Instagram. One Curepipe agency role asks for experience building communities on Facebook Groups and Reddit, plus LinkedIn and TikTok.

2. Performance marketing and paid ads

Paid media sits inside almost every generalist role. Listings name Google Ads, Facebook Ads Manager and LinkedIn Ads, and they expect you to optimise campaigns and report on results, not just launch them.

The same agency listing mentions a certification in Google Ads, Facebook Blueprint "or similar" as a preferred qualification. If you want to understand the Meta side in more depth, my guide to mastering Facebook Ads Manager is a good place to start.

3. SEO and content

SEO roles are some of the most specific. An SEO Executive listing from a local digital agency asks for keyword research, on-page optimisation, technical audits, Core Web Vitals and structured data, using tools like Google Search Console, Ahrefs, SEMrush and Screaming Frog.

Content roles overlap heavily. A Content Writer and SEO Specialist role combines writing blog posts and landing pages with schema markup, a content calendar and reporting in Google Analytics, and it asks for a portfolio of published samples.

4. Analytics and CRM

More senior roles lean on data. The Digital Marketing Executive listing in Port Louis includes defining KPIs, analysing customer and campaign data, running test-and-learn experiments and managing CRM channels such as email, push notifications and in-app messages. That's marketing automation in practice, even when the job title doesn't say so.

5. E-commerce

E-commerce roles mix marketing with operations. An E-Commerce Specialist role in Pamplemousses covers running the online store and app, campaigns on Google Ads, Facebook, Instagram, email and WhatsApp, delivery and returns targets, a customer service chatbot and compliance with the Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017.

The skills employers want for marketing jobs in Mauritius

When you line these listings up side by side, the same skills keep coming back. I group them into four layers.

1. Channel skills

Social media, paid ads, SEO, email and content. You don't need to master all of them on day one, but you should be able to run a basic campaign on at least two channels and explain your choices.

2. Tools

Across the listings I read, these names came up repeatedly:

  • Analytics: Google Analytics, Google Search Console, Meta Business Suite
  • Advertising: Google Ads, Meta Ads Manager, LinkedIn Ads
  • SEO: SEMrush, Ahrefs, Moz, Screaming Frog
  • Websites and stores: WordPress, WooCommerce, Shopify, plus basic HTML
  • Design: Canva, Adobe Illustrator

Google also offers certifications through Skillshop for products like Google Ads and Google Analytics. You earn them by completing the learning path and passing the assessment, which makes them a useful signal on a junior CV.

3. Data and reporting

Almost every role mentions KPIs, tracking and reports. Employers want people who can say what happened, why it happened and what to do next. That's the skill that moves you from "posting content" to "growing the business".

4. Languages and soft skills

Several listings call English and French fluency essential, and one lists Mauritian Creole as a plus. Communication, organisation, creativity and working across teams appear in nearly every ad too.

How to build a portfolio and get experience

Here's the catch for beginners. Employers ask for a portfolio, examples of managed communities and campaign case studies. But how do you get those before your first job?

You create them. Here's how I'd approach it.

1. Run a real project, however small

Offer to manage social media for a family business, a local association or a friend's side hustle. Set a goal, track results for a few weeks and write down what you learned.

2. Build your own website or blog

A simple WordPress site shows you can handle a CMS, write content and apply SEO basics. Connect Google Analytics and Search Console, then use real data in your portfolio.

3. Write short case studies

For each project, cover the challenge, what you did, the tools you used and the outcome. Be honest. A small result explained well beats big claims you can't back up.

4. Get certified, then prove it

Certifications show you know the theory. Pair each one with something you actually built, such as a test campaign, a dashboard or an audit, so a hiring manager can see the skill in action.

5. Learn with structure

Teaching yourself works, but it's slow and easy to leave gaps. That's why I run the Digital Marketing & AI Bootcamp with Oreegami Mauritius. It covers the channels, tools and AI skills that keep appearing in local job ads, with practical work you can put straight into a portfolio.

How AI is changing digital marketing jobs in Mauritius

AI isn't a future trend in these roles. It's already in the job descriptions.

Both of that agency's SEO listings ask candidates to understand GEO (Generative Engine Optimisation), AEO (Answer Engine Optimisation) and AI-powered search. The agency role lists experience with AI-powered marketing tools as a plus. If GEO is new to you, read my guide to generative engine optimisation.

The global picture points the same way. The World Economic Forum's Future of Jobs Report 2025 says workers can expect 39% of their existing skill sets to be transformed or become outdated by 2030. AI and big data top its list of fastest-growing skills, and 85% of employers plan to prioritise upskilling their workforce.

The same report notes that two-thirds of employers plan to hire people with specific AI skills, while 40% expect to reduce staff where AI can automate tasks.

Closer to home, the Economic Development Board points out that areas like analytics and automation are increasing demand for roles such as data analyst in the local ICT and BPO sector.

My take: AI won't replace the marketer who understands strategy, data and customers. It will replace a lot of repetitive tasks. So learn to use AI for research, drafting and analysis, and spend the time you save on thinking, testing and judgement. That combination is exactly what employers are starting to look for.

Frequently asked questions

Where can I find digital marketing jobs in Mauritius?

Local job boards such as myjob.mu regularly list roles like Digital Marketing Executive, Community Manager, SEO Specialist and E-Commerce Specialist. LinkedIn and agency websites are also worth checking, and many roles are filled through recommendations, so a visible portfolio helps.

Do I need a degree to work in digital marketing in Mauritius?

Many listings prefer a degree or diploma in marketing, business or communications, but not all require one. Some entry-level roles ask only for social media knowledge and good communication skills. Practical experience and a portfolio often matter as much as the qualification.

Which tools should I learn first?

Start with Google Analytics, Meta Ads Manager, Google Ads and Canva, then add Google Search Console and WordPress. These appear across most local listings and give you a solid base for any digital marketing role.

Is French required for marketing jobs in Mauritius?

Often, yes. Several listings describe English and French fluency, written and spoken, as essential. Mauritian Creole can also be an advantage, especially for community management and local content.

Will AI replace digital marketing jobs?

AI is changing the work rather than removing the need for marketers. Local listings already ask for an understanding of AI-powered search and AI marketing tools, so the safest move is to learn how to use AI well alongside core marketing skills.

The bottom line

Digital marketing jobs in Mauritius reward people who can do a bit of everything and explain the results. Channels, tools, data and AI: that's the stack.

You don't need years of experience to start. You need the right skills, real proof of work and a plan. Build those, and the job ads stop looking intimidating and start looking like a checklist you've already ticked.

Ready to build the skills employers are hiring for?

The Digital Marketing & AI Bootcamp gives you hands-on practice with ads, SEO, analytics and AI tools, plus portfolio work you can show employers. Start with the free pre-assessment to see where you stand, then explore the bootcamp.

02.title: How to Choose a Digital Marketing Course in Mauritius
segs:
Most people choose a digital marketing course in Mauritius the same way they choose a restaurant: a friend's recommendation, a nice-looking brochure, a start date that fits.

Then week three arrives. The slides are dense, the examples feel far from real work, and the pace is either painfully slow or far too fast.

The course wasn't necessarily bad. It just wasn't built for the way you learn.

I've trained marketing teams and career changers for years, and I've seen this pattern again and again. Two people sit in the same room, follow the same programme, and walk out with completely different results.

In this guide, I'll show you exactly what to look for before you sign up, why I think every student should take a pre-assessment first, and how my own programmes are built around that idea.

Key takeaways

  • A good course gets you working in real ad accounts, not just watching slides.
  • Look for up-to-date AI content and a trainer who still runs live campaigns.
  • Check for MQA approval: HRDC only refunds employers for programmes with prior MQA (or HEC) approval.
  • Before choosing any course, take a pre-assessment to find your learning type and starting level.
  • My free pre-assessment takes about 15 to 20 minutes and leads to a personalised learning plan.

What to look for in a digital marketing course in Mauritius

Digital marketing changes fast. A course that was excellent three years ago can be quietly out of date today.

Here are the six things I'd check before paying for any programme.

1. Practical work in real ad accounts

You don't learn Meta or Google Ads by reading about them. You learn by setting up a campaign, choosing an audience, watching the numbers move and fixing what doesn't work.

Ask the provider a simple question: will I build and manage campaigns in a real ad account during the course? If the answer is vague, that tells you a lot.

If you want a taste of what that hands-on work looks like, my guide to mastering Facebook Ads Manager is a good starting point.

2. Up-to-date AI content

AI is no longer a bonus module. It now shapes how ads are bought, how content is written and how campaigns are optimised.

A modern course should show you how to use AI tools in your daily work, and also where they go wrong. Look for topics like AI agents in campaign management, automated bidding and generative search, not just "how to write a prompt".

3. A trainer with real industry experience

There's a big difference between someone who teaches marketing and someone who does marketing every day.

Ask who will actually train you. Do they manage live budgets? Do they deal with real clients, real tracking problems and real platform changes? The best trainers bring last week's lessons into this week's class.

4. HRDC refundable and MQA approved status

If your employer is paying, this one matters a lot.

According to the HRDC eligibility rules, only employers contributing monthly to the training levy can claim, and only courses that have received the prior approval of the Mauritius Qualifications Authority (or the Higher Education Commission) qualify. The training must also be job-related and lead to new skills.

The refund itself depends on the employer's levy. HRDC's rate of refund page lists 70 to 75% of training costs for most employers, and up to 90% for courses explicitly focused on AI (up to Diploma level) from 1 July 2024, subject to the grant ceiling and scheme limits.

Always confirm the exact amount for your case directly with HRDC, and check a provider's approval status with the MQA.

5. A recognised certificate

A certificate won't make you a great marketer on its own. But a recognised one shows employers and clients that the programme met an official standard.

In Mauritius, MQA approval is the signal to look for, and as you've just seen, it's also what unlocks HRDC refunds for employers.

6. Support and feedback

Learning stalls when you get stuck and nobody notices.

Ask how feedback works. Is it one generic comment at the end, or regular, personal feedback on your actual work? Can you track your progress between sessions? Small details like these decide whether you finish strong or quietly drop off.

Before any digital marketing course in Mauritius, take a pre-assessment

Here's the part most people skip, and it's the one I care about most.

Not all students learn the same way. Some people need to see a diagram before anything clicks. Others want a clear, step-by-step structure. Some learn best by talking ideas through with others. And some only really understand something once they've done it with their own hands.

Put all four types in the same course, at the same pace, with the same feedback, and at least some of them will struggle. Not because they lack talent, but because the format doesn't fit them.

Starting level matters too. A business owner who already runs Facebook ads and a graduate who has never opened Ads Manager need very different first weeks.

That's why I believe every student should take a pre-assessment before choosing a course. It turns a guess into an informed decision.

How my free pre-assessment works

I built a free pre-assessment for anyone considering a digital marketing course in Mauritius, whether or not you end up training with me.

  • It takes about 15 to 20 minutes. Most questions are multiple choice.
  • No marketing knowledge needed. It's about how you learn, not what you already know.
  • It finds your learning type: visual, structured, social or hands-on.
  • It identifies your starting level, so you don't waste weeks on basics or get lost in advanced topics.

At the end, you get a personalised learning plan built around four things:

  1. Your learning type, so lessons and exercises match the way you absorb information.
  2. Your pace, so you move fast where you're confident and slow down where you need to.
  3. Your feedback style, so the comments you receive actually help you improve.
  4. Your personal goal, whether that's a new job, growing your own business or leading a marketing team.

You can take the free pre-assessment here. It's the single best 20 minutes you can spend before committing to any course.

Inside the Digital Marketing & AI Bootcamp

Once you know how you learn, the next question is which programme fits. My flagship is the Digital Marketing & AI Bootcamp, delivered with Oreegami Mauritius.

It runs over 20 weeks and is organised into four learning phases:

  1. Digital Foundations (weeks 1 to 4): the core concepts, platforms and customer journeys every marketer needs.
  2. Core Channels & Paid Media (weeks 5 to 10): hands-on work across the main channels, including paid campaigns.
  3. Advanced Performance & AI (weeks 11 to 16): optimisation, measurement and AI tools applied to real campaigns.
  4. Strategy & Leadership (weeks 17 to 20): planning, budgeting and leading marketing work with confidence.

Across those phases there are 20 modules. Each one comes with a presentation, reading notes, practical exercises and a revision quiz, so every learning type has something that works for them.

You also get:

  • Progress tracking, so you always know where you stand.
  • 1:1 trainer feedback on your work, shaped by the feedback style in your learning plan.
  • Flexible delivery: in-person, hybrid or online.
  • HRDC refundable and MQA approved status, which matters if your employer is funding your training.

Other programmes

If you want to go deep on one area, I also run Data & Analytics Mastery and Mastering AI Tools for Marketers. You'll find details of all three on my digital marketing training page.

Not sure which one is right for you? That's exactly what the pre-assessment is for.

Frequently asked questions

How do I choose the right digital marketing course in Mauritius?

Look for practical work in real ad accounts, up-to-date AI content, a trainer with real industry experience, MQA approval, a recognised certificate and regular personal feedback. Before you choose, take a pre-assessment to understand your learning type and starting level.

Can my employer get an HRDC refund for a digital marketing course?

Possibly. HRDC says only employers contributing monthly to the training levy are eligible, and only for courses with prior MQA or HEC approval. Refund rates depend on the employer's levy, so confirm the exact amount with HRDC.

Do I need marketing experience to take the pre-assessment?

No. The pre-assessment looks at how you learn and where you're starting from. It takes about 15 to 20 minutes, most questions are multiple choice, and no marketing knowledge is needed.

How long is the Digital Marketing & AI Bootcamp?

The bootcamp runs over 20 weeks, split into four learning phases and 20 modules. You can follow it in person, in a hybrid format or online.

What are the four learning types?

The pre-assessment identifies whether you're mainly a visual, structured, social or hands-on learner. Your result shapes your personalised learning plan, including your pace and the kind of feedback you receive.

The bottom line

The best digital marketing course in Mauritius isn't the one with the glossiest brochure. It's the one that fits how you learn, where you're starting from and where you want to go.

Check for real practice, current AI content, experienced trainers and official approval. Then start with what most people skip: understanding yourself as a learner.

Twenty minutes now can save you twenty weeks of frustration.

Find out how you learn best

In about 15 to 20 minutes, discover your learning type and starting level, and get a personalised learning plan before you choose any course. Take the free pre-assessment and start your digital marketing journey on the right foot.

03.title: Meta Conversions API Explained: Setup Guide and Pixel vs CAPI
segs:
Your Meta Ads dashboard shows a handful of purchases last week. Your shop's order list shows a lot more.

That gap isn't a glitch. It's what happens when you rely only on the Meta Pixel, a piece of code that runs in your visitor's browser and can only report what that browser lets it see.

The fix Meta offers is the Meta Conversions API, often shortened to CAPI. It sends your conversion data straight from your server to Meta, so far fewer sales slip through the cracks.

I set up tracking for businesses in Mauritius and beyond, and CAPI is the single change I recommend most often to anyone spending seriously on Meta Ads.

In this guide, I'll explain what it is, how it compares to the Pixel, the main ways to set it up, and the mistakes that quietly break it.

Key takeaways

  • The Meta Conversions API sends conversion events from your server to Meta, instead of relying only on the browser.
  • Meta recommends running it alongside the Pixel, sending the same events through both.
  • You can set it up through a platform integration, the Conversions API Gateway, server-side Google Tag Manager or a direct API connection.
  • Matching event_id and event_name on both sides stops Meta counting the same sale twice.
  • Always check your setup in Test Events and keep an eye on Event Match Quality in Events Manager.

What is the Meta Conversions API?

The Meta Conversions API is a connection between your marketing data and Meta. According to Meta's developer documentation, it lets you send events from your server, website, app or CRM so Meta can optimise ad targeting, lower your cost per result and measure outcomes.

Think of it this way. The Pixel is a reporter standing in your visitor's browser. CAPI is a reporter sitting in your back office, reading the order book.

Both describe the same purchases and leads. They just take different roads.

Why browser-only Pixel tracking misses conversions

The Pixel depends on the browser doing its job. Increasingly, browsers don't.

  • Ad blockers can stop the Pixel script from loading at all.
  • Browser privacy features can limit cookies and tracking scripts, so some sessions are never linked to an ad click.
  • iOS privacy changes give people more control over tracking, which reduces what browser-side signals can capture.
  • Technical hiccups happen too. Meta's best practices guide notes that server events can recover conversions the Pixel misses because of network issues or page loading errors.

Every missed conversion hurts twice. Your reporting looks worse than reality, and Meta's algorithm has less data to learn who your best customers are.

That second part is the one most people underestimate. If you're investing in first-party data, CAPI is how that data actually reaches your ad campaigns.

Conversions API vs Pixel: what's the difference?

This is the question I get asked most. The short answer: it's not either/or.

  • Where it runs: the Pixel runs in the visitor's browser. CAPI runs on your server or a cloud server you control.
  • What it can see: the Pixel sees on-page behaviour. CAPI can also send offline or delayed events, such as a sale confirmed later in your CRM.
  • Exposure to blockers: the Pixel is affected by ad blockers and browser restrictions. CAPI isn't loaded in the browser, so those tools don't block it in the same way.
  • Setup effort: the Pixel is a snippet of code. CAPI needs a server-side connection, though no-code options exist.

Meta's best practices recommend a "redundant" setup: use CAPI alongside the Pixel and send the same events through both. Meta's getting started guide also says to use the same Pixel ID for browser and server events.

Meta Conversions API setup: your four main options

The best option depends on your platform, budget and technical resources.

1. Partner integrations (WordPress, WooCommerce, Shopify)

If your site runs on a popular platform, start here. Meta works with partner platforms that offer built-in Conversions API connections, and the major e-commerce platforms and WordPress plugins provide ways to switch it on from their settings.

It's the fastest route for most small and medium businesses. The trade-off is less control over exactly which data is sent.

2. Conversions API Gateway

The Conversions API Gateway is a self-serve option in Events Manager aimed at marketers with some technical skill but no dedicated developers. Meta says no coding is required.

You host it in a cloud account you own, on AWS or Google Cloud, and pay only for those cloud resources or partner fees. It supports multiple domains and Pixels, and it generates the event_id deduplication key for you automatically.

3. Server-side Google Tag Manager

If you already use Google Tag Manager, Meta publishes a Conversions API Tag for server containers, available in the GTM Template Gallery.

This route needs GA4, a web container, a server container and a tagging server. It's more work, but it gives you fine control and fits neatly into an existing analytics stack.

4. Direct API integration

Here your developers connect your own server straight to Meta's endpoint. You generate an access token in Events Manager, as described in Meta's getting started guide, and send events in code.

It's the most flexible option and the right choice for custom platforms or CRMs. A few rules from Meta's API documentation are worth knowing: you can send up to 1,000 events per request, an event_time can be no more than 7 days old, and one invalid event causes the whole batch to be rejected.

Event deduplication: event_id and event_name

Here's the catch with a redundant setup. If the Pixel and CAPI both report the same purchase, Meta could count it twice.

Deduplication prevents that. According to Meta's deduplication guide:

  • The Pixel's eventID must match the server's event_id.
  • The Pixel's event name must match the server's event_name, for example Purchase on both sides.
  • Matching events are deduplicated when they arrive within 48 hours of the first event with that event_id.

Meta also describes an alternative using fbp or external_id, but notes it generally only works when the browser event arrives first. That's why I always use a unique event_id per event, generated once and passed to both the Pixel and the server.

Event match quality and customer information parameters

Sending an event isn't enough. Meta needs to match it to a real account before it can use it for targeting and attribution.

Meta's best practices explain that each server event gets an Event Match Quality score out of 10 in Events Manager, and only matched events can be used for attribution and delivery optimisation. Meta's verification guide says it generally recommends a score of 6.0 or higher.

You improve the score with customer information parameters:

  • Hash these with SHA256: email, phone, first name, last name, date of birth, gender, city, state, postcode and country.
  • Don't hash these: client IP address, client user agent, fbc and fbp.
  • Normalise before hashing: for example, trim and lowercase emails, and include the country code in phone numbers.

Meta lists email, IP address, first and last name, and phone as high-quality parameters. It also asks you to send the same customer information on the browser and server sides.

This is exactly where good data habits pay off. Businesses with rich, consented customer records, such as banks, are well placed here, a topic I cover in my article on how banks should use Meta Custom Audiences.

How to test with Test Events in Events Manager

Never assume it works. Test it.

  1. Get a test code. In Events Manager, open your Pixel and go to Test Events to generate a test_event_code, as described in Meta's API documentation.
  2. Send test events. Add the code to your server requests, or set it in your partner integration, then complete a test purchase or lead.
  3. Check both channels. Confirm the event appears from both the browser and the server, with matching names.
  4. Remove the code. Meta says to take the test code out of production payloads once you're done.
  5. Review the Overview. Meta's verification guide says events should appear within 20 minutes. Check the Event Deduplication tab and your match quality score.

Common Meta Conversions API mistakes

These are the problems I see most often when I audit tracking:

  • No deduplication. Pixel and CAPI both fire, but without a shared event_id. Results look too good to be true, because they are.
  • Mismatched event names. "Purchase" on one side and "purchase_complete" on the other won't deduplicate.
  • Unhashed or badly formatted data. Meta's parameter documentation says unhashed contact information isn't accepted, and messy formatting lowers your match rate.
  • Sending events late. Meta's best practices recommend sending events in real time or close to it, and requests with events older than 7 days are rejected.
  • Leaving the test code live. Remove test_event_code after launch.
  • Ignoring consent. Server-side tracking still needs to respect your privacy policy and local data protection law. An internal data and AI policy helps keep everyone aligned.

Frequently asked questions

What is the Meta Conversions API?

The Meta Conversions API is a server-side connection that sends conversion events, such as purchases and leads, from your server, website, app or CRM directly to Meta. It helps Meta measure results and optimise ad delivery, even when browser tracking is limited.

Does the Conversions API replace the Meta Pixel?

No. Meta recommends using both together and sending the same events through each, with matching event_id and event_name values so duplicates are removed.

What is the Conversions API Gateway?

It's a no-code option in Events Manager that you host in your own AWS or Google Cloud account. It sends web events through both the Pixel and the Conversions API and creates the deduplication key automatically.

What is a good Event Match Quality score?

Meta scores Event Match Quality out of 10 and generally recommends 6.0 or higher. Sending more hashed customer details, such as email and phone, usually improves it.

Do I need a developer to set up CAPI?

Not always. Partner integrations and the Conversions API Gateway need little or no code. Server-side Google Tag Manager and direct API integrations usually need technical help.

The bottom line

The Pixel shows you part of the story. The Meta Conversions API fills in the rest.

Run both, deduplicate properly, send clean hashed customer data and test before you trust a single number. Get those basics right and your ads finally learn from what really happened, not just what the browser saw.

Want tracking you can trust?

I set up and audit Meta Pixel and Conversions API tracking for businesses that want accurate data behind every ad decision. Send me a message here on LinkedIn and let's find the conversions you're missing.

Your Meta Ads dashboard and your order list probably don't agree.

That isn't a glitch. If you rely only on the Meta Pixel, you're relying on the browser, and ad blockers, privacy settings and simple loading errors all get in the way.

The Meta Conversions API sends your conversions from your server instead. Meta recommends running it alongside the Pixel, sending the same events through both.

In my new guide I cover:

What CAPI actually is, in plain English.
Pixel vs CAPI, and why it isn't either or.
Four setup routes: platform integrations, the Conversions API Gateway, server side Google Tag Manager and a direct API connection.
How event_id and event_name stop Meta counting the same sale twice.
Why hashed customer details lift your Event Match Quality.
How to test everything in Events Manager before you trust a number.

If you spend seriously on Meta Ads, your algorithm is only as smart as the data you feed it. Missing conversions means it learns from half the story.

04.title: How to Use ChatGPT for Marketing: 20 Prompts That Work
segs:
Most people try ChatGPT once, type "write me a Facebook post", get something bland and decide it's overrated.

The tool wasn't the problem. The prompt was.

When I train marketing teams, I see it every time: swap a vague one-liner for a prompt with context and a clear task, and the output goes from generic to usable.

ChatGPT for marketing works best when you treat it like a sharp junior assistant. Brief it properly and it saves you hours. Brief it badly and you'll spend longer fixing its work.

Below are 20 copy-ready prompts, grouped by the jobs marketers do every week. Swap the details in square brackets for your own and start testing.

Key takeaways

  • Good prompts give ChatGPT a role, context, a clear task, a format and examples. Vague prompts get vague answers.
  • The 20 prompts below cover ad copy, social media, email, SEO briefs, customer research, campaign ideas and reporting.
  • Treat every output as a first draft. ChatGPT can sound confident and still be wrong, so fact-check before you publish.
  • Feed it your brand voice so the copy sounds like you, not like everyone else using the same tool.
  • Never paste confidential information or customer personal data into a prompt.

How to write better prompts for ChatGPT

Before the prompts, a quick framework. OpenAI's own prompt engineering guidance says your prompts should be clear, specific and give the model enough context to understand what you're asking. It also recommends using descriptive words to set the tone, such as formal, friendly or humorous.

I teach a simple five-part structure that puts this into practice:

  1. Role. Tell ChatGPT who to be: "You are a senior copywriter for a Mauritian retail brand."
  2. Context. Describe your business, audience, offer and goal.
  3. Task. Say exactly what you want, in one clear sentence.
  4. Format. Specify length and structure: "5 options as a numbered list."
  5. Examples. Paste a post you love so it can match the style.

Then iterate. OpenAI describes prompting as iterative: review the answer, then adjust the wording, add context or simplify the request.

20 ChatGPT for marketing prompts that work

Each prompt follows that structure in compact form.

1. Ad copy

Prompt 1: Ad variations. "You are a performance copywriter. Write 5 Facebook ad primary texts for [business], a [type of business] in [location], promoting [offer] to [audience]. Each under 125 characters, each with a different angle." Use it when a tired ad needs fresh variations to test.

Prompt 2: Search ad headlines. "Write 15 Google Search ad headlines of 30 characters or fewer for [product] targeting people searching '[keyword]'. Include the keyword in at least 5." Use it when building a new search campaign.

Prompt 3: Offer angle finder. "Here is my offer: [describe offer]. List 10 reasons [audience] might buy it, ranked by persuasiveness, with a one-line hook for each." Use it when your ads all sound the same.

2. Social media posts

Prompt 4: Weekly content plan. "You are the social media manager for a café in Port Louis that serves office workers at lunchtime. Create a 7-day Instagram plan with one post idea, a caption under 80 words and a suggested visual per day." Use it on a Monday when you have no plan.

Prompt 5: Brand voice rewrite. "Here are three posts that represent our brand voice: [paste posts]. Describe this voice in 5 bullet points, then rewrite the following caption in the same voice: [paste caption]." Use it when your copy sounds generic and you want it to sound like you.

Prompt 6: Hook generator. "Write 10 opening lines for a short video about [topic] aimed at [audience]. Each under 12 words, designed to stop the scroll." Use it before filming Reels or TikToks.

3. Email marketing

Prompt 7: Subject lines. "Write 10 email subject lines for a [campaign type] from a boutique in Curepipe announcing [offer]. Mix curiosity, benefit and urgency, each under 50 characters." Use it when open rates are slipping.

Prompt 8: Welcome sequence. "Plan a 3-email welcome sequence for new subscribers to [business]. For each email, give the goal, subject line, a 120-word draft and one call to action." Use it when you're setting up email automation for the first time.

Prompt 9: Win-back email. "Write a friendly, short email to customers who haven't bought from [business] in 6 months. Remind them of [key benefit] and include [incentive]." Use it to reactivate past customers before paying for new ones.

4. SEO and blog briefs

Prompt 10: Blog brief. "You are an SEO content strategist. Create a blog brief for the keyword '[keyword]' aimed at [audience]. Include search intent, a title, H2 and H3 outline and questions to answer." Use it before writing or commissioning an article.

Prompt 11: Topic clusters. "My business is [business] serving [audience] in [location]. Suggest 5 topic clusters, each with one main and 4 supporting articles, based on questions my customers ask." Use it when planning a quarter of content.

Prompt 12: Meta descriptions. "Write 3 meta descriptions between 120 and 155 characters for a page about [topic]. Include the phrase '[keyword]' naturally and end with a reason to click." Use it when cleaning up pages with missing or weak descriptions.

5. Customer research

Prompt 13: Persona draft. "Based on this description of my customers: [describe], create 3 personas with goals, frustrations, objections and the words they'd use." Use it as a starting point, then check it against real customer conversations.

Prompt 14: Review analysis. "Here are anonymised customer reviews with names removed: [paste reviews]. Group them into themes and list the top 3 likes and top 3 complaints." Use it when you have lots of feedback and little time.

Prompt 15: Objection handling. "List the 10 most common objections a [audience] might have before buying [product], with a short, honest response to each." Use it when building an FAQ page or briefing sales.

6. Campaign ideas

Prompt 16: Seasonal campaigns. "Suggest 5 campaign ideas for [business] in Mauritius linked to [season, holiday or local event]. For each, give a name, core message, main channel and success measure." Use it when a key date is coming and you want more than a discount.

Prompt 17: Campaign brief. "Turn this idea into a one-page campaign brief: [idea]. Include objective, audience, key message, channels, content list, timeline and KPIs." Use it when you need to align your team or agency quickly.

7. Reporting and analysis

Prompt 18: Plain-English report. "Here is last month's campaign data with no customer details: [paste summary table]. Summarise it for a business owner in 5 plain-English bullets, ending with one recommended action." Use it when explaining results to someone who doesn't live in Ads Manager.

Prompt 19: Spot the problem. "Compare these two periods of ad results: [paste figures]. Give the 3 most likely reasons performance changed and what to check first for each." Use it when results drop.

Prompt 20: Test plan. "Based on these results: [paste summary], suggest 5 A/B tests for next month, ranked by impact and ease, each with a hypothesis." Use it to turn a report into action.

Getting better ChatGPT for marketing copy: keep your brand voice

If everyone uses the same prompts, everyone gets the same copy. The fix is to feed ChatGPT your raw material: posts that performed, the words your customers use, the phrases you'd never say. Prompt 5 is the fastest start, so save the voice description it gives you and reuse it.

Then edit like a human. Add a real detail, a local reference or an opinion only you would have. I go deeper on this in my guide to human-first content.

The limits: what ChatGPT can't do for you

ChatGPT is a brilliant drafting partner. It is not a source of truth or a safe place for sensitive data.

1. Fact-check everything

OpenAI is open about this. Its help page on whether ChatGPT tells the truth warns that it can produce incorrect or misleading answers, including invented quotes or studies, and that it might sound confident even when it's wrong. OpenAI recommends treating outputs as a first draft and verifying important information. For marketing, check every statistic, claim, price and date before it goes live.

2. Protect confidential and customer data

Never paste customer names, phone numbers, emails or confidential business information into a prompt. Anonymise first, as in Prompts 14 and 18.

Check your settings too. According to OpenAI's Data Controls FAQ, you can turn off the "Improve the model for everyone" setting so your new conversations aren't used to train its models. Temporary chats aren't used for training either, though they may be kept for up to 30 days for safety purposes.

3. Put rules in writing

Write down what's allowed, what isn't and who reviews outputs. My guide to an AI usage policy for your business walks you through it step by step.

Prompts are a start. The real gains come when your whole team can brief AI well and review its output. That's what I cover in Mastering AI Tools for Marketers, where teams practise on their own campaigns.

Frequently asked questions

How do I use ChatGPT for marketing as a small business?

Start with repetitive jobs: social captions, ad variations, email subject lines and blog outlines. Give it a role, context, a clear task and a format, then edit the output into your brand voice.

Can ChatGPT write my marketing copy for me?

It writes strong first drafts, but always review them. OpenAI warns it can be confidently wrong, so check facts and add details only you know.

Is it safe to put customer data into ChatGPT?

Avoid it. Don't paste personal or confidential data. Anonymise first, review your data control settings and set clear rules for your team.

What makes a good ChatGPT prompt?

A clear, specific one with a role, context, the exact task, a format and ideally an example of the style you like. Then refine it based on the first answer.

The bottom line

ChatGPT for marketing isn't magic, and it isn't a gimmick. It's leverage, and the quality of what you get depends on the quality of your brief.

Use these 20 prompts as a starting kit. Keep your voice, check your facts and protect your customers' data, and you'll win back time for the work that needs you.

Want your team using AI properly?

I help businesses train marketing teams on AI and automate the repetitive work that slows them down. Explore Mastering AI Tools for Marketers or send me a message here on LinkedIn and let's find where AI can save you the most time.

Sources

  • OpenAI Help Center: Prompt engineering best practices for ChatGPT
  • OpenAI Help Center: Does ChatGPT tell the truth?
  • OpenAI Help Center: Data Controls FAQ

Most people who say ChatGPT is useless for marketing have only ever typed one vague line into it.

The tool isn't the problem. The brief is.

When I train marketing teams, the biggest shift comes from one habit: giving ChatGPT a role, context, a clear task, a format and an example. The output goes from generic to genuinely usable.

So I've put together 20 copy ready prompts grouped by the jobs marketers do every week: ad copy, social posts, email, SEO briefs, customer research, campaign ideas and reporting. There are local examples too, like a café in Port Louis and a boutique in Curepipe.

Used well, it's leverage. Used badly, it's extra work.

05.title: Google Business Profile Setup and Optimisation for Small Businesses
segs:
Someone in Grand Baie types "seafood restaurant near me" into Google. Three businesses appear on the map. They pick one, tap "Directions" and they're on their way.

If your restaurant isn't one of those three, you never even had a chance.

That's the power of a Google Business Profile for small business owners. It's free, it sits on Google Search and Maps, and it's often the first thing customers see about you. Sometimes instead of your website.

Yet I still see Mauritian businesses with unclaimed listings, wrong hours and unanswered reviews.

In this guide, I'll show you how to set up Google Business Profile step by step, how to optimise it, which mistakes to avoid, and a checklist you can work through this week.

Key takeaways

  • Your profile only appears to customers after you verify it, so verification is step one, not an afterthought.
  • Use your real-world business name. Adding keywords, taglines or locations to the name breaks Google's guidelines.
  • Pick the most specific primary category you can. Categories affect your local ranking.
  • Ask every happy customer for a review, reply to them, and never offer incentives for reviews.
  • Google says you can't pay for a better local ranking. Complete, accurate, active profiles win.

Why a Google Business Profile for small business owners matters

Google explains that local results are based mainly on three things: relevance, distance and prominence.

You can't move your salon closer to every customer in Rose-Hill. But you can control relevance and influence prominence through reviews and ratings.

Google is also direct on one point: there's no way to pay for a better local ranking. It's about doing the basics better than the business down the road.

There's a newer reason too. AI search tools draw on local business data when they answer questions like "best salon in Rose-Hill". A complete, consistent profile gives them accurate facts to work with. I cover that shift in my guide to generative engine optimisation (GEO).

How to set up Google Business Profile: step by step

1. Create or claim your profile

Sign in to a Google Account (Google suggests using your business email domain if you're creating a new one), then go to the Business Profile create page and type your business name. Google's setup guide walks you through category, location, service area, phone and website.

If your business already shows on Maps, you'll be asked to claim it rather than create a new one. If someone else has already verified it, such as a former employee or agency, you can request ownership. According to Google, the current owner has 3 days to respond, after which you may be able to claim it.

Note that profiles are for businesses with in-person customer contact. Online-only businesses aren't eligible.

2. Verify your business

Google states that customers can only find your profile after you complete verification. The available methods can include phone or text, email, a live video call, a video recording or a postcard. Google chooses which ones you're offered, and you can't change that.

A few practical rules from Google's help page:

  • Postcard codes usually arrive within 14 days and expire after 30 days.
  • While you wait, don't change your name, address or category, and don't request a new code.
  • Reviews of verification can take up to 5 business days.
  • Never share your code. Google says it will never ask you for it.

3. Use your real business name, nothing more

This is where many small businesses go wrong. Google's guidelines for representing your business say your name should reflect your real-world name, the one on your signage and stationery.

Taglines, phone numbers, URLs, opening hours and location details aren't allowed. So if a hypothetical restaurant is called "Lagoon Grill", that's the name. "Lagoon Grill Best Seafood Restaurant Grand Baie Mauritius" is keyword stuffing, and it puts your profile at risk.

4. Choose your primary and secondary categories

Your primary category should be the most specific option that describes what your business is. Google's own example: choose "Nail salon" rather than "Salon". Google also confirms that the categories you select affect your local ranking.

Additional categories are for real departments. A Rose-Hill beauty salon might choose "Beauty salon" as primary and add "Nail salon" if it genuinely runs one. Don't add a category for every product.

5. Set your address or service area

If customers visit you, add your exact address. P.O. boxes and virtual offices aren't eligible.

If you travel to customers, like a mobile hairdresser, hide your address and set a service area instead. You can add up to 20 areas by city or postal code, and Google suggests staying within about 2 hours' drive of your base. Hybrid businesses can show both.

6. Add accurate hours

Enter your regular customer-facing hours, then use special hours for public holidays. In Mauritius, that saves a lot of customers from turning up to a closed door.

7. Write your description and attributes

Your business description can be up to 750 characters. Google asks you to leave out URLs and HTML and to focus on the business itself, not promotions or prices.

Then add attributes such as Wi-Fi or outdoor seating. Google notes that some attributes may help you appear in searches for places that have them.

Google Business Profile optimisation: making your profile work

1. Add real photos and videos

Google recommends a logo, a cover photo and business photos, including an exterior shot so people recognise you on arrival. Its photo and video guidelines ask for JPG or PNG files between 10 KB and 5 MB, ideally 720 px by 720 px, and videos up to 30 seconds long and 75 MB.

Keep them real. Google advises against heavy filters. Show the actual sunset terrace, the actual stylist at work, the actual plate.

2. List your products and services

Use Edit services to pick from Google's suggestions or add custom services with a short description. A Rose-Hill salon could list "Keratin treatment", "Bridal makeup" and "Gel manicure". Keep custom service names free of phone numbers and prices.

3. Publish posts and updates

Posts come in three types: updates, offers and events. A restaurant can post a live music night or a weekend special. Google archives posts older than 6 months unless you set a date range, so a stale profile looks exactly that: stale.

My advice: plan one post a week. It keeps your profile visibly alive.

4. Collect reviews the right way

Google's review tips suggest sharing a link or QR code with customers. Put the QR code on the bill folder, the salon mirror or your WhatsApp follow-up message.

What you can't do matters just as much. Google's contribution policy prohibits offering discounts or free services for reviews, asking only happy customers (review gating), and reviews from staff or family because of conflict of interest.

5. Reply to every review

Google advises short, specific replies that use the reviewer's name, sent promptly. For negative reviews, acknowledge genuine mistakes, avoid personal attacks, and move complex issues to phone or email.

6. Check how customers can message you

The old built-in chat feature is gone. Google confirms that chat ended on 31 July 2024. For eligible accounts, customers can now contact you from your profile through text messages or WhatsApp. If that option shows in your dashboard, turn it on, then make sure someone actually answers.

7. Use performance insights

Your Performance page shows views, the search terms people used to find you, direction requests, calls, website clicks, messages and bookings. Check it monthly.

If people search "nail salon Rose-Hill" but you never mention nails, you've found a gap. To connect those clicks to real sales on your website, you'll want proper tracking and first-party data in place.

Common Google Business Profile mistakes to avoid

  • Breaking the guidelines and getting suspended. Google says it may suspend profiles that don't follow its guidelines. If it happens, don't create a new profile. Fix the issue, gather evidence such as business registration and utility bills, and appeal once, carefully.
  • Duplicate listings. Google allows only one profile per business. If you move premises, update your existing address rather than creating a new profile, and don't create separate profiles for each service.
  • Fake or incentivised reviews. Google removes them, and they damage trust with real customers who can often spot them.
  • Inconsistent name, address and phone. Keep them identical on your website, Facebook page and Google profile.

Google Business Profile for small business: optimisation checklist

  1. Profile claimed and verified
  2. Real-world business name, no extra keywords
  3. Specific primary category, a few relevant secondary ones
  4. Correct address or service area
  5. Regular and public holiday hours up to date
  6. Description written, attributes ticked
  7. Logo, cover, exterior and interior photos added
  8. Products or services listed
  9. One post a week
  10. Review QR code in use, every review answered
  11. Name, address and phone identical across the web
  12. Performance insights checked monthly

Frequently asked questions

Is a Google Business Profile for small business owners free?

Yes. Creating and managing a profile is free, and Google states that you can't pay for a better local ranking.

How long does Google Business Profile verification take?

It depends on the method Google offers you. According to Google, verification reviews can take up to 5 business days, and postcard codes usually arrive within 14 days.

Can I add keywords to my business name on Google?

No. Google's guidelines say your name should match your real-world business name. Adding taglines, locations or service keywords isn't permitted and can lead to suspension.

Can I run a profile if I don't have a shop?

Yes, if you serve customers in person. Service-area businesses hide their address and list up to 20 service areas instead. Online-only businesses aren't eligible.

Can I offer a discount in exchange for a Google review?

No. Google prohibits incentives such as discounts, free products or payments in exchange for reviews. You can, and should, ask every genuine customer for honest feedback.

The bottom line

A Google Business Profile for small business owners is the closest thing to a free shop window on the busiest street in town.

Set it up honestly, keep it complete, and show up every week with photos, posts and replies. The businesses that win local search in Mauritius won't be the biggest. They'll be the most consistent.

Want more customers from local search?

I help businesses in Mauritius and beyond get found locally, from Google Business Profile and local SEO to ads and tracking that show what's really driving calls and visits. Send me a message here on LinkedIn and let's make your business the one people choose.

Yet I keep seeing unclaimed listings, wrong opening hours, keyword stuffed business names and reviews that never get a reply.

Google is clear on a few things. Your profile only shows once it is verified. Your name must match your real signage. Your primary category affects your local ranking. Offering discounts for reviews is prohibited. And there is no way to pay for a better local ranking.

06.title: WhatsApp Business Marketing: Turn Chats into Sales
segs:
Here's a question I ask every Mauritian business owner I work with: where do your sales actually close?

Almost every time, the answer is the same. Not on the website. Not in the shop. On WhatsApp.

In my article on the digitalised bazaar, I showed how sellers take buyers from a TikTok live straight into WhatsApp to close the deal by hand. It works. But it's also chaos: missed messages, forgotten follow-ups and no idea which post or ad brought in the sale.

That's where WhatsApp Business marketing done properly changes things. Same chats, same customers, but with structure, automation and numbers you can trust. Here's how to set it up, step by step.

Key takeaways

  • The WhatsApp Business app is free and built for small businesses. The WhatsApp Business Platform is for medium and large businesses that need scale.
  • A complete profile, a tidy catalogue, quick replies and labels turn a messy inbox into a sales pipeline.
  • Ads that click to WhatsApp on Facebook and Instagram send people straight into a chat with you.
  • You need clear opt-in before sending marketing messages, and you must honour every opt-out.
  • Track every chat from first message to sale, or you'll never know which marketing pays.

WhatsApp Business app vs WhatsApp Business Platform: which do you need?

The WhatsApp Business app

According to the official WhatsApp for Business FAQ, the app "is for small businesses to communicate with customers from a single device." It's free to use, with limited customisation and integration with other tools.

If you're a boutique, a caterer or a live seller handling your own chats, start here. No technical setup needed.

The WhatsApp Business Platform (API)

The same FAQ says the Platform "enables medium and large businesses to chat with customers at scale through programmatic access to WhatsApp." You either sign up directly as a developer or work with an approved Business Solution Provider, who may charge for their own services.

My rule of thumb: if one or two people answer every chat, use the app. If you need several agents, automated flows, order updates from your systems or proper conversion tracking, move to the Platform.

It doesn't have to be all or nothing. Meta's coexistence documentation explains that app users can connect their existing number to the Cloud API through a partner and keep chatting in the app. Some features, such as broadcast lists, become read-only, so check the details first.

Set up WhatsApp Business so it sells for you

Most businesses add a logo and stop there. Here's what I recommend instead.

1. Complete your business profile

WhatsApp calls the business profile a "virtual storefront" for your logo, description, hours and website (WhatsApp Business app features).

Fill in every field: what you sell, where you deliver and how people can pay.

2. Build a catalogue people can shop

The catalogue is a mobile storefront inside WhatsApp. You can group items into collections, share catalogue links on WhatsApp, Facebook and Instagram, and let customers send you a cart in a single message (WhatsApp).

WhatsApp's own guidance is to give each item a clear name, consistent photos, a short description, a price and details such as sizes or lead times.

For live sellers, that means one link instead of typing the same price over and over.

3. Automate greeting and away messages

A greeting message welcomes new customers when they first message you. An away message replies automatically outside your business hours (WhatsApp).

Use the greeting to share your catalogue link. Use the away message to say when you'll be back.

4. Save quick replies for common questions

Quick replies are saved shortcuts you send in a few taps. WhatsApp suggests them for pricing, payment methods, pickup details, return policies and out-of-stock updates (WhatsApp).

Their recommended structure: a personal greeting, one direct answer, a next step and an optional catalogue link. I'd add one thing. End with a question that moves the sale forward, such as "Which size would you like?"

5. Use labels as your sales pipeline

Labels let you sort and filter conversations (WhatsApp). I think they're the most underrated feature in the app. Create labels that match your sales stages:

  • New lead: asked a question, no order yet
  • Quote sent: price or catalogue shared
  • Awaiting payment: order agreed, not paid
  • Paid: ready to deliver
  • Repeat customer: bought before

Now filter "Quote sent" every evening and follow up. That one habit recovers sales most businesses never knew they lost.

Drive chats with ads that click to WhatsApp

Ads that click to WhatsApp "send people that click on your ads directly into conversations with your business in WhatsApp," according to Meta's developer documentation. They run on Facebook and Instagram, with image, video, carousel and slideshow formats.

When someone taps, a chat opens with a pre-filled message. You can customise it, add an automated greeting with buttons and offer up to three icebreaker questions (Meta).

Three tips from running these campaigns:

  1. Match the ad to the first reply. If the ad promotes a product, your greeting should show that product and its price.
  2. Use a different pre-filled message per campaign. "Hi, I saw the Diwali offer" tells you exactly which ad brought the chat in.
  3. Staff the inbox. Paying for chats you answer hours later is the fastest way to waste budget.

On the Platform, there's a cost bonus too. If someone messages you from one of these ads and you reply within 24 hours, Meta opens a 72-hour free entry point window in which messages are free (Meta pricing documentation).

New to Meta campaigns? My guide to Facebook Ads Manager covers the basics.

WhatsApp Business marketing messages: opt-in, consent and no spam

The WhatsApp Business Messaging Policy says you may only contact people who gave you their number and agreed to receive your messages. You must also respect every request to block or opt out, whether it comes on or off WhatsApp.

What a valid opt-in looks like

According to Meta's opt-in guidance, your opt-in must state that the person is agreeing to receive messages over WhatsApp, and it must name your business. You should also explain how to opt out of specific types of message.

You can collect opt-in on your website, in a chat, by SMS, by phone or on paper in your shop. Meta recommends separate opt-in for different types, such as order updates and promotions.

How marketing messages work on the Platform

A 24-hour customer service window opens when a customer messages you. Outside it, you can only send template messages (Meta). Templates fall into marketing, utility and authentication categories, and each must pass review before you can send it (Meta).

On pricing: since 1 July 2025, Meta charges per message, with rates that vary by message category and the recipient's country (Meta). Replies inside an open service window are free, but marketing templates are always charged, so check the current rate card for your markets.

Broadcast without becoming spam

In the app, Business Broadcasts let you send private one-to-one messages to many people at once, with scheduling and insights, for eligible users in select countries (WhatsApp).

Whichever tool you use, the policy is blunt: people should expect your messages, and you must not "spam, or surprise people" (WhatsApp). Blocks and reports can limit how many messages you can send.

My best practice:

  • Only message people who opted in, and record when and how.
  • Segment by label, so repeat customers get loyalty offers and new leads get introductions.
  • Send less often, but make every message worth opening.
  • Offer a simple way out, such as "Reply STOP to stop offers," and honour it immediately.

Consent is also the start of your own customer data, which is why I pair it with a zero-party data strategy.

How to measure WhatsApp Business marketing results

If you can't connect a chat to a sale, you can't tell which marketing works.

1. On the app: labels plus a simple log

Use your pipeline labels and keep a basic sheet: date, source, product, value and status. Ask every new lead how they found you, and use a unique pre-filled message, QR code or short link per campaign. WhatsApp lists QR codes and short links as free ways to start chats (WhatsApp).

It's manual, but you'll finally see which sources bring orders.

2. On the Platform: send conversions back to Meta

The Conversions API for Business Messaging lets you report events that happen in the chat, such as LeadSubmitted, QualifiedLead and Purchase, back to Meta. Each chat from a click-to-WhatsApp ad carries a click ID that ties it to the ad.

Meta also offers purchase optimisation for these ads, so the algorithm looks for buyers, not just people who say hello.

Frequently asked questions

What is WhatsApp Business marketing?

It's using WhatsApp Business tools, from your catalogue and labels to ads that click to WhatsApp and opted-in messages, to win leads, close sales and track results from chat to sale.

Is the WhatsApp Business app free?

Yes. The app is free. The Platform has no access fee, but Meta charges per message depending on type and country, and partners may add fees.

Can I send promotional messages to anyone on WhatsApp?

No. WhatsApp's Business Messaging Policy only allows you to message people who gave you their number and agreed to hear from you, and you must honour every opt-out.

Do ads that click to WhatsApp work with the free app?

Yes. WhatsApp lists them among the paid options for app users. For deeper tracking, you'll need the Platform.

How do I track sales that close on WhatsApp?

On the app, label each sales stage and log every lead's source and value. On the Platform, send purchase events to Meta with the Conversions API for Business Messaging.

The bottom line

Your customers already want to buy on WhatsApp. The question is whether you're running it like a stall or like a business.

Good WhatsApp Business marketing comes down to three things: a setup that sells, permission you can prove and numbers you can trust. Get those right and every chat becomes a step towards a sale.

07.title: AI Automation for Local Businesses: 7 Processes to Automate First
segs:
It's 9pm. A potential customer has just sent you a WhatsApp message asking if you have a slot on Saturday.

You're tired, you'll reply tomorrow. By tomorrow, they've booked with someone else.

If you run a small business in Mauritius, you know this feeling. The work isn't the problem. It's the hundred small admin tasks around the work: replies, reminders, invoices, spreadsheets.

That's exactly where AI automation for business earns its keep. Not robots replacing your team, but simple systems that handle the repetitive bits.

In this guide, I'll show you the seven processes I'd automate first in any local business, how to start without breaking anything, what you should never automate, and how to stay on the right side of Mauritian data protection law.

Key takeaways

  • AI automation for local businesses works best on repetitive, rule-based tasks like replies, reminders, invoicing and data entry.
  • Start with the process that loses you the most customers or time, usually lead follow-up or enquiry replies.
  • Pick one process, map it, automate it, measure it, then expand. Don't automate everything at once.
  • Keep humans in charge of sensitive decisions, complaints and anything that needs empathy.
  • Any automation that touches customer data must respect the Mauritius Data Protection Act 2017.

Why AI automation for local businesses matters now

Small businesses everywhere are moving quickly on AI. In the US, the U.S. Chamber of Commerce reported in 2025 that 58% of small businesses say they use generative AI, up from 40% the year before.

Mauritius has its own context, but the pressure is the same: customers expect fast answers, and small teams can't be online all day and night.

Here's my view: most local businesses don't need a big AI project. They need two or three well-chosen automations that quietly remove friction every single day.

7 processes to automate first with AI automation for business

These are the processes I see slowing down shops, clinics and service businesses across Mauritius again and again.

1. Lead capture and follow-up

The problem: Leads arrive from your website, Facebook, Instagram and word of mouth. Some sit in an inbox. Many never get a follow-up.

What the automation does: Every new lead lands in one place automatically, gets tagged by source, and receives an instant acknowledgement. If nobody has replied after a set time, the system reminds your team or sends a polite follow-up.

Tools to look at: a web form connected to a simple CRM and an email tool, linked with a Zapier or Make style connector.

The benefit: No lead falls through the cracks, and people hear from you while they're still interested.

2. Enquiry replies on WhatsApp and email

The problem: The same questions arrive every day. Opening hours. Prices. Location. Do you deliver to Curepipe? Answering each one by hand eats your day.

What the automation does: Common questions get an instant, accurate answer, and anything complex is passed to a person. The WhatsApp Business app already includes greeting messages, away messages for outside business hours, quick replies and labels. An AI assistant can go further by drafting replies from your own FAQ for a team member to check and send.

Tools to look at: WhatsApp Business messaging tools, email templates and filters, and an AI assistant trained on your approved answers.

The benefit: Customers feel looked after, even at 9pm, and your team spends its time on the conversations that really need them.

3. Appointment booking and reminders

The problem: Back-and-forth messages to find a time, double bookings and no-shows.

What the automation does: Customers pick a free slot themselves, get a confirmation straight away, and receive reminders before the appointment, with an easy way to reschedule.

Tools to look at: an online booking tool synced to your calendar, plus email or message reminders.

The benefit: Fewer messages, fewer gaps in your diary and a more professional first impression.

4. Invoicing and payment reminders

The problem: Invoices go out late. Chasing payments feels awkward, so it gets postponed. Cash flow suffers.

What the automation does: When a job is marked complete, an invoice is created and sent automatically. If it isn't paid by the due date, a friendly reminder goes out on a schedule you control.

Tools to look at: accounting or invoicing software with recurring invoices and automatic reminders, connected to your CRM or job tracker.

The benefit: Steadier cash flow and no more uncomfortable chasing conversations.

5. Reporting dashboards

The problem: Every month someone copies numbers from five platforms into a spreadsheet.

What the automation does: Data from your ads, website, sales and bookings flows into one live dashboard. An AI assistant can then summarise what changed and flag anything unusual.

Tools to look at: a dashboard tool connected to your ad accounts, analytics and spreadsheets, with connectors filling the gaps.

The benefit: Decisions based on current numbers, not last month's guesswork. If you run paid campaigns, this is also the foundation for the kind of setup I describe in AI agents for campaign management.

6. Social media content drafts

The problem: You know you should post regularly. But staring at a blank screen every week means it rarely happens.

What the automation does: An AI assistant turns your product updates, offers and customer questions into first drafts of posts and captions. You edit, approve and schedule.

Tools to look at: an AI writing assistant with your brand guidelines, plus a scheduling tool for your social channels.

The benefit: A consistent presence without starting from zero each time. Keep a human edit in the loop: your voice and local knowledge are what make content worth reading.

7. CRM data entry and updates

The problem: Customer details live in WhatsApp chats, email threads and someone's memory. Updating the CRM by hand is boring, so it doesn't happen.

What the automation does: New contacts, bookings, purchases and invoices update customer records automatically.

Tools to look at: a CRM with built-in integrations, connected to your forms, booking tool and invoicing software.

The benefit: One reliable view of every customer, which makes follow-ups, offers and service far easier. It also builds the first-party data your future marketing will depend on.

How to start small with AI automation for business

The biggest mistake I see is trying to automate the whole business in one go. Here's the approach I recommend instead:

  1. Pick one process. Choose the one that costs you the most customers or the most hours. For many local businesses, that's lead follow-up or enquiry replies.
  2. Map it. Write down every step as it happens today: who does what, in which tool, and where things get stuck.
  3. Automate the repetitive parts. Keep the steps that need judgement with a person. Test with a few real cases first.
  4. Measure it. Compare response times, missed leads or late payments before and after.
  5. Then expand. Once the first automation runs smoothly, move to the next process on the list.

Before you go further, set some ground rules for your team. My guide to writing an AI usage policy for businesses is a good place to start.

What not to automate

Automation isn't a substitute for judgement. Keep these with a human:

  • Sensitive decisions, such as credit, hiring, pricing exceptions or anything with a significant impact on a person.
  • Complaints and difficult conversations, where empathy matters more than speed.
  • High-value relationships, like key clients and partners who expect to hear from you personally.
  • Anything you can't explain. If you don't understand why the system made a decision, don't let it make that decision alone.

Rule of thumb: automate the admin, not the relationship.

Data protection: keeping automation compliant in Mauritius

Almost every automation in this list touches personal data: names, phone numbers, emails, appointments and payments.

In Mauritius, that means the Data Protection Act 2017 applies. According to the Data Protection Office, the Act came into force on 15 January 2018, and anyone who holds information about individuals must comply with its data protection principles.

The Data Protection Office website also covers registration, your legal obligations and individuals' rights, including access, rectification, erasure, the right to object and a specific section on automated individual decision making. That last one is directly relevant if you let a system make decisions about people.

In practice, before you switch on any automation:

  • Collect only the data the process really needs.
  • Tell customers how you use their data, and get consent where it's required.
  • Check where each tool stores data and who can access it.
  • Never paste sensitive customer information into AI tools your business hasn't approved.

If you're unsure, check the Data Protection Office guidance or speak to a legal adviser.

Frequently asked questions

What is AI automation for business?

It's the use of software and AI tools to handle repetitive tasks automatically, such as replying to common enquiries, sending reminders, creating invoices and updating customer records, so your team can focus on work that needs human judgement.

Which process should a small business automate first?

Start with the process that loses you the most customers or time. For most local businesses, that's lead follow-up or replying to enquiries on WhatsApp and email, because speed of response directly affects sales.

Do I need technical skills to automate my business processes?

Not for the basics. Many booking, invoicing and CRM tools include automations out of the box, and connector tools let you link apps without code. For more complex workflows, it helps to get support from someone who has set them up before.

Is AI automation legal under Mauritian data protection law?

Yes, as long as you handle personal data in line with the Data Protection Act 2017. That means respecting its principles and individuals' rights, including those around automated decision making. The Data Protection Office website is the official reference.

Will automation replace my staff?

In my experience, no. The goal is to remove repetitive admin so your people can spend more time on customers, sales and service, the parts of the business that really need a human.

The bottom line

AI automation for business isn't about doing everything with AI. It's about choosing the right first process and doing it well.

Start with one. Map it, automate it, measure it. Keep people in charge of the decisions that matter, and respect your customers' data.

Do that, and the 9pm message never goes unanswered again.

Ready to automate your first process?

I help local businesses in Mauritius map their processes and set up practical AI and business process automation, from lead follow-up to reporting. Send me a message here on LinkedIn and we'll find the right place to start.
